passage:
In the canteen of their Hyderabad school, Irawati announced it with total confidence: "The board is cancelling practical exams this year. It's confirmed."
Asif stopped eating. "Who confirmed it?"
Irawati opened her mouth, and nothing came. She had heard it so many times that it felt as solid as the times table. Was it a teacher? A cousin?
That night she scrolled back through the family group. There it was, forwarded four times by different relatives, in red capitals: "BREAKING! SHARE WITH ALL STUDENTS." No name, no notice number.
The next morning the class teacher pinned up the real circular: practicals as usual, in March.
Irawati found Asif at the gate. "I only believed it because I kept seeing it. I didn't even remember where it came from."

qa.q: What did the class teacher's circular say?
qa.a: Practicals as usual, in March.

qa.q: Why did Irawati feel so sure the practicals were cancelled?
qa.a: She had seen the claim so many times that it felt as solid as the times table, even though she could not remember where it came from.

qa.q: What was Irawati's turning point, and what could she do next time?
qa.a: Being unable to answer Asif's "Who confirmed it?"; next time she could ask herself that before repeating a claim and look for an official notice.

qa.q: How might Asif have been affected if he had believed Irawati?
qa.a: Asif might have stopped preparing for the practicals and been caught out in March because of a forward.

grounding: It shows a teenager repeating a claim as fact because it feels familiar, having forgotten it came from a forwarded message.

passage:
"Ma, don't cook that rice," Rafiq said from the kitchen door. "They're making fake rice out of plastic now. You can bounce it like a ball."
His mother, Vinita, kept stirring. "Who told you?"
"Everyone knows it."
"Everyone who?"
Rafiq thought. "I've heard it loads of times."
"Heard it, or read it?"
He pulled out his phone and scrolled. "Here. The colony group. And here, the cricket group. And here, from Nanu." Three forwards of the same video.
"So one video, three times," Vinita said. "Did anyone test it? Or say where it came from?"
Rafiq read them again. "No." He rubbed his neck. "It just felt true because I kept seeing it."
"Then let's roll a ball of this rice after dinner and see if it bounces."

qa.q: Where had Rafiq seen the fake rice claim?
qa.a: In the colony group, the cricket group and a forward from Nanu, the same video three times.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq say, "Everyone knows it"?
qa.a: He had seen the claim so often that it felt like common knowledge, and he had forgotten it all came from one forwarded video.

qa.q: Which question from Vinita changed Rafiq's thinking?
qa.a: "Heard it, or read it?" made him check his phone, where he found one video forwarded three times with no source or test.

qa.q: How might Vinita feel when Rafiq says it only felt true because he kept seeing it?
qa.a: She may feel relieved that he noticed it himself, which is why she turns it into a playful rice test instead of a lecture. 😊

grounding: It shows a teenager treating a repeated forward as common knowledge until a parent's questions bring back its source.

passage:
Last month I nearly got Darshan into serious trouble, and I still wince about it. I told our whole tuition batch that Darshan had copied the science project from the internet. I said it like a fact. I believed it.
When Darshan asked me, shaking, "Who said that?", I realised I didn't know. I'd heard it so many times that it just felt true. I went back through my phone and found it: an anonymous message someone had forwarded to the batch group weeks earlier, "Darshan's project is copied lol". That was all. No proof. By the fourth time it reached me, I'd forgotten it was ever just a forward.
I said sorry to Darshan in front of the batch. Now, before I repeat anything, I ask myself one thing: where did I actually hear this? I'm Urmila, and I'm trying.

qa.q: What did the anonymous forwarded message say?
qa.a: It said, "Darshan's project is copied lol."

qa.q: Why did Urmila believe the claim about Darshan?
qa.a: Urmila felt certain the claim was a fact after hearing it so many times, and now feels ashamed, having forgotten it began as one anonymous forward.

qa.q: What question does Urmila now ask before repeating something?
qa.a: Urmila asks, "Where did I actually hear this?", which brings back the lost source before a claim spreads further.

qa.q: What was it like for Darshan to hear the rumour?
qa.a: Darshan was shaken at being accused in front of the batch with no proof, which is why an apology in front of the same batch mattered.

grounding: It shows a teenager who repeats a rumour as true because it feels familiar, having lost track of the forwarded message it came from.

passage: Observation note, Class 10 study hall, Thursday. During free period, Imran told his study group, very firmly, that the board had scrapped practical exams this year, so nobody needed to finish lab files. Two students closed their files. When I asked where he had read it, he said, "Everyone knows, Ma'am, I've seen it so many times." He could not name a source. I asked him to scroll back through his phone with me. The line turned up four times, each a forward from different family groups, never from the board's own notice page. He went quiet, then said, "I really thought a teacher told us." We opened the official circular together: practicals are on. He went back to the group and corrected himself. I have asked him to lead a five-minute check-the-source talk next week. — Usha Menon, class teacher

qa.q: How many times did the claim about practical exams turn up on Imran's phone?
qa.a: It turned up four times, each a forward from different family groups.

qa.q: Why did Imran feel sure the practicals were scrapped, even without a source?
qa.a: He had seen the line so often that it felt familiar, and that familiarity felt like proof; he even thought a teacher had told them.

qa.q: What habit could help Imran the next time a claim feels obviously true?
qa.a: Before repeating it, he could ask himself where he first saw it and open the official notice, the way he and his teacher did together.

qa.q: How were the two students who closed their files affected by Imran's confidence?
qa.a: They trusted him and stopped working on their lab files, so a rumour spoken as fact could have left them unprepared for real practicals.

grounding: The note shows a teenager passing on a forwarded claim as fact because repeated sightings made it feel true, without recalling where it came from.

passage:
Tuesday night
Big embarrassment at tuition today 😖
I told Trisha, like it was settled news, that the city is draining Ambazari lake next year to build a car park. I even said it in front of Sir. Trisha asked, "Who said?" and I said "It's everywhere, yaar." She said, "Where exactly?"
And I couldn't answer. I honestly felt like I had read it in the newspaper. Then on the bus I scrolled back. It was in our society group. Then the cousins' group. Then someone's status. Same forward, same blurry photo, four or five times. No newspaper at all.
The weird part is it still feels true when I think of it. Hearing something again and again sort of glues it in.
New rule for me: before I say "everyone knows", I check who actually said it.
— Ojas

qa.q: Where did Ojas actually find the claim about the lake when scrolling on the bus?
qa.a: In the society group, then the cousins' group, then someone's status: the same forward four or five times.

qa.q: Why did Ojas feel as if the story came from a newspaper?
qa.a: Seeing it so many times made it feel familiar and solid, and the forward's real origin had slipped from memory, so it felt like proper news.

qa.q: What turning point stopped Ojas from spreading it further, and how can it be kept up?
qa.a: Trisha's simple question "Where exactly?" made Ojas check; keeping the new rule of checking who said it before saying "everyone knows" builds on that.

qa.q: How might Trisha see Ojas after asking "Who said?"
qa.a: Trisha probably wasn't trying to embarrass Ojas, only to know if it was real; the question saved them both from believing something with no source.

grounding: The diary shows a teenager repeating a claim as fact because it felt familiar, then finding it came only from repeated forwards.
